utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, good afternoon to you. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Oric, and good afternoon to you too. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, and also good afternoon to the Defence. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I'm here together with co-counsel, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you, Mr. Wubben and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour; good afternoon, my learned friends. My name is Vasvija Vidovic. Together with Mr. John Jones, I appear for Mr. Oric. With us are our legal assistant, Ms. Adisa Mehic and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam, and good afternoon to you and your team. Just two small things: Number one is that I have just signed before entering the courtroom an order pursuant to your Defence response to Mr. Nikolic's motion, giving the Prosecution, should you wish to respond to any of the matters raised by the Defence, up to today week, Wednesday, and Mr. Nikolic or his Defence team the same. In other words, I'm giving him - or them - the opportunity to respond by Wednesday. Because even if you leave the matter more or less in our hands, you do raise some issues that I think ought to be addressed, if not by the Prosecution as such, at least by Mr. Nikolic himself, all right? Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We already received the motion filed by Defence yesterday, and indeed we intend to -- at least to do an oral submission or probably a written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you want to make an oral submission, you are free to do so, but to be honest with you, Mr. Wubben, although I'm not trying to discourage you, I would rather use the time that we have to make sure that we finish with this witness, rather than -- it's up to you if you want to make an oral --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't mean to do it by today, but in one of the coming days or beginning next week. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's it. The other thing is we are now in a position to draft the decision on Rule 68. We've finished discussing. So but I haven't started drafting as yet. So it will take me at least until tomorrow to finish the drafting. That's the second thing I wanted to tell you. Right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: In respect to the latest issue, we would like to do a short, a limited oral submission, and I request Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio to do so, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio, by all means. In the meantime, we were informed today that, after all, Prosecution did discover the second page of that newspaper article or report that you copied us yesterday. I take it that you have received it. Yes. Mr. Di Fazio, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours; and thank you, the Defence. If Your Honours please, I've got a translation that I can provide to you of the -- which is a translation of the page that Ms. Vidovic had yesterday, and the second page that we have now discovered. And I need to address you because of certain matters, and it may also have an impact on your decision as well. So I think it's best that I address you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yesterday, Ms. Vidovic said, referring to the part of the newspaper article that she did have - and remember that this article was generated following last week's Rule 68 issue - we went out and did an extra search and we came up with that article. And Ms. Vidovic says: "So from this part you can see that the units of the Red Berets under the command of [this gentleman] were present on the Drina front throughout the war, which we have been proving and which all of the Prosecutor's witnesses that we questioned about the Red Berets denied." That's what's in her transcript. And I think, with respect, she's right. I think that can only be categorised as another Rule 68 sentence in this newspaper article. I'm not trying to shy away from that. So -- and that's why I wanted to raise it with you now. Your Honours then went on to ask me: "Is the entire article in your possession?" And I replied: "That's exactly my point. That's exactly my point." Your Honour said: "If you don't have it, obviously I can't ask you to go and get it." And then I went on to a submission regarding whether or not the Defence accepts what we say to them. The point is I'm concerned that I may have misled you, because in fact we were in possession of it, although yesterday I didn't know that and I didn't believe that we were in possession of that. And so it's important that you understand, A, that it contains Rule 68 material, that sentence. In respect of this newspaper article, I'd like to adopt all of the submissions that I made in respect of the other material, insofar as prejudice is concerned, and I'd like to adopt them. In my submission, the amount of Rule 68 material in this particular article is so minimal and so - how to put it? - it's not particularly usable for cross-examination purposes in the sense that it's so distant from the events; it's third, second, fourth-hand material, obviously. And so therefore, the Prosecution's submission is that on the issue of prejudice, the Defence have not suffered much. Essentially the same submissions that I made to you last week. Now, why was this not generated by the search that we conducted last week following the initial Rule 68 controversy, so to speak? And I raise that only because of the other issue that's concerned, systematic failure or disorder on the part of the Prosecution's case that's leading to this sort of thing. If Your Honours please, and if you look at the documents -- do Your Honours have the B/C/S and the English now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Good. Thank you. First of all, the ERN numbers, if you look at the page that the Defence had yesterday, that's the first page of this article, it ends with the ERN number 3320. Right? Then the second page, which is what was disclosed last night, ends with the ERN number 3322. It's not in sequence. We've looked at the computer records that we have, and it's clear that these two sequential pages were entered into the Evidence Unit on the same day, but as different documents. When the search was conducted last week for this man -- on this man, the search was refined as best it could be to Slobodan Misic, Top. If you look at the second page, that's the one ending 22, you've only got Misic, which is a very -- it's a pretty -- if you use that name, it will generate thousands and thousands of documents. So the refined search didn't pick up the second page that was entered separately. Furthermore, the IIF or the MIF that accompanies the entering of these documents into the Evidence Unit did not have any keywords that would have revealed Misic or Slobodan or Top and that's why the second page was not discovered. One would have expected, if the job had been done properly, that the two documents would have been entered as the one range, so they would have had the one range under the one MIF or IIF document and that would have meant that the entire article was put in and rendered -- it would have resulted -- a proper refined search would have come up with the whole thing. So that's the mechanism by which the initial search we did last week didn't come up with this particular document. The second submission that I want to make about it is that if you look at the English translation, if Your Honours please, the article -- and it's got all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. -- Usher, please. Be kind enough to go to the witness and explain to him that we'll be with him pretty soon, that we are discussing something which does not relate to him. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right. It's got -- it's a whole series of articles. If you look at the B/C/S version, you can see that it's two pages, so to speak, with different articles. The big one -- the main article is that one that you can see, headed -- and I asked the translators to put in the B/C/S headline at the top so you can see which particular headline -- which translation relates to which particular article. The Rule 68 material is in the article headed "'Top' was not in the Red Berets."

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That page, 3320, if you read the English translation, okay, it ends at about the end -- the end of the second paragraph, beginning of the third paragraph. In fact, you can see the words -- yeah. The English paragraph: "It is obvious that ..." Sorry, third. "It is obvious that Misic would not have met any of those conditions." Do Your Honours have that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All of that that follows is on the second page from that point on in the English. He says then that there is -- he was personally in command of actions in the areas of Visegrad, Srebrenica, and Bratunac. Now, that would also constitute Rule -- I suppose Rule 68 material. But any prejudice that's been caused in the intervening week is minimal, because the first page has really got the gravamen, the heart of the matter. That's where the real stuff is. That is the "commander of the majority of actions carried out at the Drina battlefield." Do you see that in the first paragraph? So the fact that this other page was disclosed later has not, essentially, worsened the situation any more than it was from last week. And furthermore, the search that the Prosecution conducted following last week's Rule 68 controversy was, in the circumstances, completely reasonable, sensible, and the fact that it didn't produce this second page is the result of a quirk or an anomaly that occurred when the person who entered it into the Evidence Unit put in a second page of a newspaper article as a completely separate document; and furthermore, nothing in the IIF would have come up on the search material. So I just wanted to add that, those comments to you, so that you -- in case you need to adopt or use any of this material for purposes of your decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you in a position to tell us what was ERN number 3321?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. I've seen it. It's another B/C/S series of -- it's a page, a B/C/S page, with a number of articles that don't deal with this, so I'm told from our B/C/S interpreter. It's not a continuation, as far as I can understand, of the first page, 3320, and then you have 33 -- 3321 is not a continuation of this 3320, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can't, of course, force the Prosecution to show us a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm willing to do that, Your Honours. And if the Defence want --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I was careful in the words that I chose.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If the Defence wants that page, we'll hand it over. It's not a problem at all. We'll just disclose it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. Ms. Vidovic or Mr. Jones, whichever of you, do you wish to address this matter any further?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, no, not in any depth. We wouldn't propose a point-by-point rebuttal of the points made by Mr. Di Fazio just now. We adopt certainly our submissions on prejudice and systematic failure for all the documents so far which have been in discussion. We say this document, it speaks for itself in terms of its exculpatory nature. In terms of prejudice, we would just say this: That we did put to Prosecution witnesses that there were Red Berets and each one of them denied it. We would have had, if this had been disclosed in due timely fashion, we would have had this document and we would have had the information which is contained about Red Berets and about the names of commanders of the Red Berets, et cetera, to put to those witnesses. So generally, as with the other documents, we've been deprived of the opportunity of making effective cross-examination using documents rather than simply putting propositions without being able to back them up. And I'd finally just say this on institutional failure on the part of the Prosecution: That the Prosecution's approach seems to be that -- to this issue, that it's simply a matter of searches, of putting in terms into a big search engine. The fact is the Prosecution is a body which has institutional knowledge and must be presumed to have a certain amount of institutional knowledge. It has a Prosecutor at its head, it has senior trial attorneys, investigators, analysts, and certainly, in our submission, many of those persons in the Office of the Prosecutor will have relevant institutional knowledge about the Misic case, and also on other exculpatory issues. Certainly we would imagine they can be consulted. Obviously, I don't teach the Prosecution their job or presume about how they conduct their affairs. But it seems always to be a case of putting in search terms and then the explanation that there are these huge archives. Well, the fact is it is an Office of the Prosecutor headed by a person, with people working there, and those people, I presume, are also Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. being consulted on the Slobodan Misic case, because it's a case, it's not just a search term. It's a case, and there are leads which could have been followed up concerning the witness statements which were taken in Serbia in relation to that case. But apart from that, we simply stand by the submissions which we've already made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. And I hope next time we'll speak on this will be in our decision, of course, but I hope you realise, both of you, and particularly the Prosecution, why we have and still do take this matter extremely seriously. We have a responsibility to make sure that you meet with your obligations and that the rights of the Defence are fully respected. But over and above that, we also have a responsibility to ensure and maintain the integrity of the cases that we are dealing with. And my concern - and when I say "mine," I'm not speaking for myself only; I'm speaking for Judge Eser and Judge Brydensholt, in the most open manner - is that even the events pertaining to this singular incident itself reveals one very important aspect: That we started from one step and we ended up a few steps higher, resulting in the disclosure of fresh documents. In other words, we ended up -- the situation where initially there was only one document, not having been disclosed, and ending up with having more documents, or discovering more documents not having been disclosed. And again, between yesterday and today, a second page pertaining to a document that now has been -- has come to the surface. Of course, no one attributes, and I don't think even the Defence has attributed bad faith to you. I mean, I don't think I've heard any suggestion that you have acted maliciously. But on the other hand, please, Mr. Wubben, Mr. Di Fazio, I cannot impress enough because I do not find the right words here and now and I want to start with the witness, I cannot impress enough with you the importance of thoroughly searching, again and again and again, as the case goes by, the fresh, incoming documents. And when I say thoroughly, I mean thoroughly. I know you have four million documents-plus, but it's your responsibility, and no one is going to do the work for you. And if you don't, and at the end of the day, when the cooking process has come to an end, you discover that you have forgotten to put in one or more fundamental ingredients, you will end up with something that you will not like. Some things you can replace. If you have forgotten to put salt, you can put it later; if you have forgotten to put spices, maybe you can give it a little bit of reheating and add spices; or if you have forgotten pepper, you can add pepper. But if you have forgotten the basic ingredients, at that point, what you have is not edible, or if it is eaten, it will not be as good as it would be. And I think I have made myself understood. Anyway, tomorrow or the day after we'll come down with our decision, but in the meantime, please do understand that the question of Rule 68 disclosure does not begin and end during the pre-trial stage; it continues throughout, and periodically, as documents move from one section of this Tribunal to another, you need to update and make sure that everything is disclosed. Because we can come up to a stage where it is too late to address any major damage or prejudice that could be caused. So let's bring the witness, please, and I thank you for your cooperation on this. We'll have the same schedule as yesterday, Madam Vidovic, so we stop at 4.00 and then we continue at half 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are we ready? Yes, Mr. Ademovic. Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry to have kept you waiting, but it was a matter that we needed to discuss which does not involve you and that we needed to conclude the exchange of submissions on it, and it had to be done today. Good afternoon, once more. I hope you have had a good rest and that you are fresh enough to continue with your examination-in-chief. I'm just going to remind you that you are testifying under oath, or in terms of the solemn declaration that you entered yesterday. We are not going to repeat it. It's still applicable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I understand everything. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ademovic.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you and to all present.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher to show the witness two documents together; document 04381963 and document 04381966, because these documents are connected. And finally, I will ask a single exhibit number for both documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll start with that. This will become D845, 845.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me describe the documents, since it is two documents in one, please, Madam Vidovic. All right. This document which is being tendered as one document by the Defence and marked as D845 consists of the following: The first part of this document is in B/C/S is -- consists of two pages with ERN 04381963 to 964, followed by three pages in B/C/S with ERN number 04381966 to 968. Each one of these texts is accompanied by the corresponding translation into English. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I only wish to establish whether the witness is receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because we are now getting it on channel 3 instead of 6, as it appears to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I was just about to intervene and say I had no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please just change the channel, or I don't know how we're going to regulate this, but there's no Bosnian interpretation on channel 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, we have to establish. Now, Mr. Ademovic, are you receiving interpretation now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. On which --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, now I am, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On which -- on channel 6. So basically I will repeat two things to you. First, what I told you yesterday: If at any time there is a problem with the interpretation, draw my attention immediately, because I am not in a position to know that. I mean, I'm only listening in English on channel 4. I'm not following in Serbo-Croat as well, and I can't do that. So if that happens again, please tell me straight away, all right? That's number one. Number two, we haven't asked you any questions. I was just describing this document for record purposes, and this document is being entered as Defence Exhibit D845. Do you want me to give him more information than that? I don't think so. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Just one matter. I just can't quite understand why it's getting the one exhibit number. I've got the English translations. They appear to be separate documents. I wondered if the Defence wanted to give them separate numbers. One appears to be command of the East Bosnia Corps, 6th of July, and the other one appears to be analysis of combat activities report. And I -- unless there's going to be evidence that they're all attached and part of the one document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. Di Fazio. I can't answer that question. I had a specific request from the Defence to have them entered as one document, so I didn't argue, of course, with the Defence. Maybe they deal with the same incident or -- the question is -- the request to have them entered as one document came before the questions, so usually I would intervene after having heard the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. If it's the case of having them entered separately, I will tell you, Ms. Vidovic. I mean, I will not hesitate in doing that. For the time being, we'll have them as one document. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. It will soon become clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please look first at document 04381963.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document issued by the command of the East Bosnia Corps, under strictly confidential number 11/2-933, and it's dated the 6th of July, 1992. The title is "Analysis of combat activities, hereby submitted to the commands of all units." I will quote only paragraph 1, which says: "On the 13th of July, 1992, starting at 0800 hours, an analysis of combat activities for the previous 30 days will be held at the corps command. Commands of brigades and other independent units will attend the analysis, as will the corps command bodies." Witness, please pay attention to the number of this document in the heading. It says "11/2-933." Do you agree that this part of the document speaks of the preparation of a meeting at which combat activities will be analysed?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what the document shows.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now please look at this other document, and it bears the number 04381966, and the title is "Analysis of combat activities report." And I will quote the beginning of this document. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: "Pursuant to your document strictly confidential number 11/2-933, dated the 6th of July, 1992, we hereby submit to you the following report: "1. The most frequent form of combat activities in the previous time period. From the beginning of combat activities in the area of responsibility of the Birac Brigade, we conducted combat activities while surrounded, simultaneously with coordinated activities with aviation, organised attacks and a breakthrough from the surrounding area. We conducted these combat activities supported by aviation and our own artillery." In connection with this part of the document, I wish to ask you the following: Can you confirm that the document number 11/2-933, dated the 6th of July, 1992, is the same number contained in the heading of the command concerning the analysis of combat activities, which you have just seen and which was delivered to the commands of all units?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are the same numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And in connection with this, I will ask you as follows: Did you know that in the area where you were, in Susnjari and its general area, the Birac Brigade was operating?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My area, the area of Susnjari, belongs to the Birac area.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And how did you receive this information?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had this information through my Motorola, where I listened in to their conversations.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned this Motorola yesterday. I would now like to dwell on it a little bit. Could you tell Their Honours what kind of Motorola this was and what its range was.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a small hand-held Motorola. Its range was four to five kilometres, as the crow flies. And if there are no hills around, then it has a range of four to five kilometres. However, if there are any physical obstacles, then the range is somewhat less.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours for what purposes you used it as a policeman before the war?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For local contacts in town, to get information from my colleagues or the police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the range of this small Motorola was four to five kilometres. Was the Serb army within that range?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we look at the map, Ravni Buljim, point 820, and Rogac, as the crow flies, the distance is four to five kilometres. Jezestica, from Lupoglava, my position at Jaglici, the distance is about two or two and a half kilometres, and to Siljkovici it's about two kilometres. To the centre of Kravica, it's about four kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is this, then, how you got information about the Birac Brigade and its combined activities with artillery and aviation?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please turn to page 2 of this document, document 04381967. That's the end of this page, under number 6, reads as follows: "Within the area of responsibility of the brigade, there are currently three groups of volunteers who have agreed to fight under the joint command. These are mostly men with war experience from Croatia. They have been used to occupy certain elevations and for combat in populated areas." My question to you, in connection with this, is: In July 1992, did you have any experiences with these volunteers which you said you knew were fighting in this area? I mean you personally.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the Buljim area, from the direction of Jezestica and from the direction of Lipenovici because the territory of Buljim is elevated, and this is wild, broken countryside.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information about some of them being killed there?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember any of them?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. More than once, we clashed with them, when refugees went from the direction of Susnjari towards Konjevic Polje, on the 29th of June, one of them was killed at Hajducko Groblje. And then on the 6th of August -- on the 6th of August, and previously, before that, there had been fighting. I remember one of them was from Nis, another one was from Sabac. On the 29th of June, we confiscated an M-53 from him and --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. And another question in connection with this: To the best of your knowledge, were they under the command of the local Serb army? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In these clashes with Serbs in the Jezestica area, did you get hold of any weapons?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, on the 29th of June, we took an M-53 and a combat kit with ammunition. We also took some light infantry weapons from them, also certain parts of uniforms, and there were times when we would get seven or eight rifles, whether PAP or automatic rifles, from them, because they would throw them away when they were wounded and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, because these two documents are mutually connected, that was why I asked for them to be given a single number. Now you can put these documents aside, Mr. Ademovic, and I would like to ask the usher to show the witness another document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is document -- a document issued by the Birac SAO, Bratunac municipality, garrison command of the 1st of July 1992, and the title is "Bringing up to manpower levels the combat units of Bratunac municipality." The document number is 04361487. And the first page of this document -- Witness, if you have received the document, please turn to page 2 right away. Page 2 is numbered 04361485, and it says: "Code-name overview, strength of units on 26th of June, 1992." And Witness, please look at the lower part of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I want to make sure, Ms. Vidovic, and in this way I'm addressing the witness directly, that in looking at this page 2 that is ending with ERN 1485, since most of it is handwritten and a copy that I have, at least, leaves much to be desired. It's none of your fault, but you can barely read what's written there. I want to make sure that the witness is in a position to read it, in other words, to distinguish the letters there. If he's not, I would suggest that we put the original on the ELMO and then we zoom in the parts that you want the witness to address, and we see whether that will make it better for him. Because as it is, for example, if you ask me whether I'm reading the first eight, I can barely distinguish the letters.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes. For the first eight, that is true. However, the one that is relevant to us is quite legible, at least my copy is. I don't know about the witness's. Because I'm interested in number 10 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you read what is stated there under number 10 and onwards, and if you can read the columns there?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I can, and if I have some doubts, I will let you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that we could place the document on the ELMO. I don't see any reason why not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Madam Usher, if you put the -- and could the technicians please focus on the last 15 entries and zoom in, if at all possible. Zoom in where the names are first, and then, if necessary, we'll move to the right -- to the left, all right? That should make it better for you, Mr. Ademovic. If you look at the monitor instead of the paper, you should see better. All right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... question, Madam Vidovic. I hope I have helped you in this way. I didn't mean to interrupt you, I meant to help.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could you please scroll the paper -- the document down in order for us to see the headings of the columns. So we would like to see the upper part of the document. Thank you very much. Perhaps if you could move it to the left. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you see that there, under the title "Overview, strength of units," it says here officers, junior officers, soldiers, total. Then there is AP, then PAP. Do you see these columns? Do you see the columns where it says "AP" and "PAP," where it is written "men, officers, junior officers, soldiers"?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do see it now. I apologise. I could not see it on the screen before that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I will quote parts of the document for you. If we could look at the bottom part of the document now, please, if the usher could assist us, where it says: "The Bratunac unit of the Serbian army." And if you could look at number 10. Do you agree with me that it is indicated here KDA TO?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is to say, TO Command. Please look at number 11. Do you agree with me that it is stated here "the TO detachment number 1"?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please focus on the most relevant part now, under number 13, TO Detachment Kravica. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the line below, the Drina Detachment. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In connection with this, I want to ask you the following: On the 26th of June, 1992, did you know about the existence of the Drina Detachment?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I've already stated so. On the basis of the information provided to me by the refugees who fled from the area of Drina in the direction of Zvornik. Their centre of activity was in the area of Slapasnica. I apologise. This is the detachment that operated along the Drina River, around Ljubovija, in the direction of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your earlier testimony, on several occasions you mentioned Kravica and stated that people there were armed and well-equipped. Did you know that at the end of June 1992, they had a TO detachment in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at number 13, where it is stated "Kravica" and then the columns "men," "soldiers," "total."

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please move it. Can we see the bottom part?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Under "total," it is stated 430. In late June 1992, did you know how many soldiers there were in the area of Kravica?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We knew that the areas of Kravica, Jezestica, and Sekovici had hundreds of them, the area in the direction of Rogac.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that they had automatic weapons?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the column where it is stated "infantry weapons, AP-80." What does "AP-80" stand for, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Meaning?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it means that we had 80 automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Look at PAP-287. Can you tell us what this stands for?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Semi-automatic rifle. Therefore, they had 277 [as interpreted] semi-automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it seems that something else is entered into the transcript. My question was: How many automatic weapons were there in Kravica? And the witness answered that they had 80 automatic weapons. The way it is entered into the transcript, it seems as if we had 80 automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Witness, please, who had 80 automatic rifles that are indicated in this document?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Kravica TO Detachment. I said that the Serbs, who were part of the Kravica unit, had these weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This served to correct the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, as for the rifle 7.9 millimetres-141, what does that stand for?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, and according to what is stated here, these are M-48 rifles of long and longer range.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: According to this document, how many are indicated here?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, 141.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Next, there is SNP-6. Do you know what the "SNP" abbreviation stands for?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sniper.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does it, therefore, follow from this document that this particular detachment had six snipers?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then it says "PM-16."

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are light machine-guns.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: According to this document, would then this mean that they had 16 light machine-guns?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please decipher the following row. Please take a look at it, the one following the heading "PM." Would you please take a look at the column. Can you decipher the one next to the one with the heading "PM"?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, it says "TMS" or "TRS" and "APC."

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, and can you see how many APCs are indicated here?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. The next column has the heading "MB." What does that stand for?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the military term for mortar.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: According to this document, how many mortars did they have?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, can you tell us whether Jezestica is a hamlet of Kravica?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In connection with the document you have just been shown, I have a question to ask of you. According to this document, the inhabitants of Kravica had some 500 rifles, including automatic weapons; they had light machine-guns and mortars. Can you tell us the following: Does this document reflect the actual situation in the Kravica area in terms of weaponry, in light of your experience connected with the attacks from the Kravica area?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were very well organised, equipped, and coordinated with the other Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, the question and the answer that has now been given indicates that the inhabitants of I think Kravica -- I can't see that in the document. I thought it was a TO that we were talking about. I wonder if it could be indicated where it says that the inhabitants had these documents. Thanks -- these weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you. It calls for an explanation, Madam Vidovic. Because if you look at the second page, that is ERN 1485, under number 13, it says "TO Kravica." I don't know if the first one is [B/C/S spoken]. I don't know what that is. CD or -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to thank my learned colleague from the OTP, but I never mentioned the population of Kravica. I mentioned the Kravica area. I asked whether Jezestica was part of the Kravica area, and according to this document, whether the Kravica area had these weapons. I never mentioned the population itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, I thank you for your explanation, which I do not doubt in the least, especially since you have Mr. Jones sitting next to you. But Mr. Jones can also confirm that the transcript doesn't tell you that, and I'm not saying that you are wrong. Line 15, please. According to this document -- this is your question: "According to this document, the inhabitants of Kravica had some 500 rifles, including ..." et cetera, et cetera. So that's what the transcript says. I want to make sure that when -- I want to make sure that there was no misunderstanding between you and the witness. We're not talking of the inhabitants of Kravica as having 500 of these different kinds of weapons. We're talking of the TO of Kravica. So basically the question that you need to answer is whether, basing yourself on your own personal knowledge of the events at the time, you can confirm or you can agree with Madam Vidovic's suggestion to you that the TO in Kravica had at its disposal something like 500 automatic weapons, or these kind of weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Territorial Defence of Kravica had these particular quantities. That's what I was referring to, to the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. Okay. I thank you. That's clear enough, Madam Vidovic. Let's move ahead. Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio, for raising that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You understood me as discussing the TO Kravica?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If someone were to claim, even at the time when this document was drafted on the 26th of June, 1992, that in Kravica and its hamlets of Jezestica, Siljkovici, Colakovici, Mandici, Popovici, and so on, these inhabitants only had village guards, would that be true? I mentioned the inhabitants now.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Quite the contrary, because the village guards are something completely different. They consist of smaller, disorganised groups that are not coordinated with others. They are not well equipped. And they possibly have some sports or hunting weapons. Whereas here we clearly deal with a well-organised, well-equipped, well-coordinated units, both locally and in the general area, which form part of the system, and I repeat: The system.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In June and July of 1992, did you perceive these to be village guards? You were out in the field.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were well organised and they were part of the Serbian army. In all the segments of the military doctrine.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could Your Honours please -- this document be assigned a number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic. This document, which consists in the original B/C/S language, of three pages, with ERN 04361484 to 486, plus then the corresponding translation into English, which for you -- reasons of tabulation, consists of six pages, is being tendered and marked as Defence Exhibit D846.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ademovic, you noticed that four mortars were indicated as Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. existing in the Kravica area on the 26th of June, 1992, according to this document. Do you know where these weapons were deployed?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew their precise location. One of them was in Stara Jezestica. I can even tell you under which tree it stood. It was a walnut tree. Another one was in the Kajici area, about one kilometre away from the Bratunac-Kravica main road. The third one was in the Cirkovici area, and the fourth one was on the bus station plateau in the centre of Kravica -- or rather, the fourth one.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can we only enter into the transcript that the third one was, as the witness said, was in Siljkovici, not in Cirkovici. S-i-l-j-o-k -- i-c. To your knowledge, what was the target of these artillery weapons?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They attacked at Cizmici, Bljeceva, Glogova, and the wider area of Pobrdze.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Apart from these artillery weapons, were there other artillery weapons that you knew of and which also acted -- fired upon your area?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which ones?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were weapons of larger calibres, in the Brezik area, brigade and corps artillery of various calibres, on the Rogac plateau.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher now please show the witness another document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document issued by the command of the 4th MAP, of the 10th of October, 1993, and it concerns background information for the celebration of the forming of the Drina Corps, and the number is 04342994. Mr. Ademovic, first of all, do you know what "MAP" stands for?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mixed artillery regiment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, for the record, just because I don't know whether you said the 4th or the 5th, but on the transcript, in the transcript, it says 4th MAP, while the document says 5th MAP. I just wanted to correct that. You can proceed, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would there be a pause between question and answer, interpreters note. The speakers frequently overlap.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: "The 5th MAP was formed on the same day, the 26th of January, 1993, when the Drina Corps was established by order of the main staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. The basis for forming the regiment was a mixed artillery group which had in turn grown from 122-millimetre self-propelled gun battery. On the 24th of June, 1992, this battery, its men and equipment, was relocated from Sarajevo to Milici, whereupon it was immediately included in combat operations." Please turn to the next page. Under number 4: "Following its redeployment from Sarajevo to Milici on the 24th of June, 1992, the SH battery was immediately thrown into battle and contributed to the defence of the bauxite mine from the Turkish forces. No subsequent operation took place without a crucial role being played by this artillery unit. It was mainly engaged on the forward front line from which it engaged targets directly." Mr. Ademovic, yesterday you mentioned that your areas were targeted by artillery from Milici. Is it or is it not correct that all infantry attacks on your area were supported by artillery, including artillery from Milici?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that I have already mentioned this more than once. In early June, even when there was no infantry activity in our area of Susnjari, Pobrdze, long-range artillery was still firing, and now I see what it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may we have an exhibit number for this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic. This document, which consists of two pages in B/C/S, with ERN number 04342994 to 2995, and the corresponding translation into English on two pages, is being entered and marked as Defence Exhibit D847.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Would the usher please show the witness D760.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is document 04382030. The document is issued by the East Bosnia Corps Command, dated the 28th of July, 1992, and addressed to all units. The title is "Order, active firing." I will now quote the document to you: "I hereby order all units shall set ambushes on a daily basis, infiltrate the rear of the enemy, infiltrate sabotage groups, with a view to discovering the disposition, inflicting losses, and the cutting off particular roads along which the enemy moves. In regular reports, report on the above tasks. And finally, all units in their areas are to cut off all routes used by the enemy." In connection with this, I will ask you the following,

utterances.speaker: MR. ADEMOVIC
utterances.text: Does this order reflect what was actually happening in late July and early August 1992 in your area?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And who attempted to move around in the Ravni Buljim area?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The road running through Ravni Buljim was the only corridor through the rugged terrain used by the unfortunate refugees, whose numbers grew daily and who were attempting to reach Konjevic Polje. With these ambushes, the last exit open to these desperate people was closed, and I experienced this in my own area. If I may only add -- I do apologise: These desperate people, in their thousands, were shelled in the fields by this artillery from Rogac and other areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry. I just want to be sure that I'm following this evidence, if Your Honours please. I'm not objecting to anything. But D760, I understand -- the document was presented to this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: -- and asked if, you know, it reflects the situation, yes, the answer was yes, and then the question was: "Who attempted to move around in the Ravni Buljim area?" I'm not following something here on this document. I can't see anything about Ravni Buljim. If -- I'm sure that Madam Vidovic wasn't making any leading questions or suggesting any answers there, so I wonder if the document has been finished or if there is a connection between D760 and Ravni Buljim, then you should know about it. Otherwise, how would you evaluate this evidence? Does Your Honour understand?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I understand you. Yes, Ms. Vidovic. I think there is an explanation for it, basically. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yesterday we mentioned the Ravni Buljim area at least five times. It's the only area through which the refugees moved on their way to Konjevic Polje. The witness explained that this was the only exit available to them. So I can't go back and repeat all of yesterday's testimony. If one was following what the witness was saying yesterday, then this document and what the witness said is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. As I understand it, Mr. Di Fazio -- I don't know, maybe this will help close this matter. As I understand it, what Madam Vidovic is trying to find out from the witness, seek from the witness, is a confirmation that as a result of these ambushes, the only way out, only route available for these refugees to reach Konjevic Polje -- safely Konjevic Polje was being blocked or being made -- this is what -- how I understand it. If I am not understanding you well, please correct me straight away. I don't know. But that's how I have understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No problem with that, and I heard the evidence yesterday and I understood. You remember, the witness drew a little map and did the circle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What I fail to see is the connection between this document and that evidence yesterday, and that's what I'm asking about. The evidence is coming forth to you in a manner such that D760 is somehow connected to this route in that area. Now, how and why?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because it seems to be -- and again, I am not offering evidence, I'm just trying to explain to you why I did not encounter the same problem that you seem to have. Basically, if you look at D760, it does say that: "Different groups should infiltrate, or with the aim of discovering the schedule of the enemy, to cause losses to the enemy and to block some roads where the enemy is moving." Before, it says: "All units will set ambushes every day and infiltrate the rear of the enemy." So -- and the document ends up with: "All units should block in their areas all the roads where the enemy is moving." This seems to presume that when they speak of enemy, enemy could include refugees. I mean, basically we're talking of enemy being the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: We may be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, it may be. It may also be [indiscernible]. But you have to concede that enemy here is used on very generic terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: But that's not really the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, but it seems to be to all units. So all units would include also the units that were operative in that area. That's the way -- that's why I didn't stop this series of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: As I said, I've got no objection. The witness can be asked about the area that he's talking about at length and give all sorts of answers. That's not objectionable. And the issue of whether the enemy consists of civilians and/or fighters or a combination or it's got some other meaning, that's not, with respect, Your Honour, not the issue either. The issue is only this: How do we know, how will you eventually know when you come back to read this evidence that D760 concerns an area called Ravni whatever it was and not Osmace or not Suceska or not Kravica or not Fakovici or some other area. That's all I'm concerned about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. Because at the very top of the document you have an indication that this document comes from the command of the East Bosnian Corps, and it is addressed to the -- all the units, to the command of all the units. So if you have any doubt as to whether this area fell under the jurisdiction or operative jurisdiction of the East Bosnian Corps, of course, you are right. But if you don't have a reason to doubt that, I mean, it's difficult to envisage how this document does not cover that area too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I certainly accept that it covers this area, but what I can't understand is how it doesn't cover other areas. However, in the interests of time, I won't pursue this matter any further and I'll deal with it in cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Vidovic, please forget this and move to your next question, because we need to move. I think we are moving very slowly.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if the Prosecutor needs to clarify certain points, he can do so in the cross-examination. He's taking up a lot of time in this way. I was about to move on in connection with this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ademovic, please, you understood my question, and in connection with that, I will now ask you the following: Yesterday you mentioned the village of Brosevici. What happened in the village of Brosevici in this period?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the document, and according to what I experienced in the field, what is reflected here is the implementation on the ground. On the 28th of July, the village of Brosevici was attacked, the people expelled, the houses burnt or torched, part of the inhabitants and refugees arrived in my area of Susnjari, Jaglici and Brezova Njiva, and another part went in the direction of -- Hovici [phoen] --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And two other villages the interpreter did not hear.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It says here: "All units in their areas are to cut off all the roads used by the enemy in late July." What did this mean for you, and did this actually happen in your area?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What you just said refers to closing the last exit open from the Susnjari region, through the Buljim area, towards Kravica, or rather, towards Konjevic Polje. It was now definitely closed. And we were completely surrounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Madam Vidovic. Judge Eser would like to put a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just for the matter of clarification: Could you please circumscribe what you think was the territory of the East Bosnian Corps. Which territory belonged to the command of the East Bosnian Corps? Could you please describe it on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness will have problems because the East Bosnia Corps covers East Bosnia. We have only a small part of it on the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. In fact, that is what I'm telling Judge Eser, that it's probably much -- it goes much beyond what we have on this map, because that is only part of East Bosnia. So as I understand it, Judge Eser, I mean, I am not an expert on these matters, but the East -- when we speak of the command of the East Bosnia Corps, we're talking of an area which is a vast area, which comprises the totality of East Bosnia. That's how I understood -- I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: But if this is true, then it's really the problem that the command is comprising a very large area, and the document we are dealing with doesn't refer to any place. Now, the problem is: How can we -- how can the witness know that the places, the villages which he mentioned, are exactly those which are referred to in this document? I hope you understood my question. If --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have understood your question, but I had my Motorola, and I listened in to their communications. I mentioned that their relay equipment had been set up. It was a whole system on the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Rogac plateau, not just one relay station, and I was able to see it with the naked eye. I can indicate it to you on the map. Elevation 820, Ravni Buljim, where I was, and Rogac face each other, and they're about three and a half to four kilometres apart as the crow flies. And you can see the antenna with the naked eye, because they are large objects which are easily visible. So I listened in on my Motorola and I understood every detail of what is under discussion here. Because I knew well who belonged to whom and who was subordinate to whom.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it says here quite clearly that the document is addressed to all units.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something? Excuse me, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's close -- are you satisfied, Judge Eser? Yes. Then we move to the next question, please, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Could I have the usher's assistance and show D75, a Defence exhibit. D75.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is the directive of the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army for further operations, number 3, signed by the commander of the Republika Srpska army, General Ratko Mladic. It was drafted on the 3rd of August, 1992, and bears the number 00876215 up until 6227. Witness, could you please turn to page 2. In the Bosnian version there is one virtually empty page and then there is page number 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the English version, that is page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Or rather, could you please turn to the next page in the B/C/S version. It might be page 3, where it is stated: "I have decided ..."

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 3, under 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. It says: "Operation objectives." And it is somewhere in the middle that it says: "Crush Ustasha forces in the area of Birac and the general area and crush the forces in the areas of Birac, Visegrad, Gorazde, Trnovo and the wider area of Foca and secure land communications with Herzegovina from Eastern and Central Bosnia." And then, under 5 -- turn to the next page, where it says: "Unit tasks." And then turn to page 5, where it says: "East Bosnia Corps. Secure the area along the right bank of the Sava River, and the forces in coordination with the 1st Krajina Corps should liberate Majevica, Semberija, and Birac, from the Ustasha forces." Please then look at paragraph 2, the last sentence in the second paragraph, where it says: "In the Birac area, disarm or crush the remaining Ustasha forces." Can you find that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which paragraph, the number of the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I apologise. Which page is that?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 5, paragraph 53.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've found it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have to lower -- yes, that's it. All right. Thank you, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was quoting as follows: "With part of forces, secure the territory along the right bank of the Sava River and with the main forces, in coordination with the 1st Krajina Corps, liberate Majevica, Semberija, and Birac from the Ustasha forces." My question to you is the following: The Serbs, when they said "Ustasha forces," who did they mean by "Ustasha forces"?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They meant the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the Muslims, how did they call them?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Turks or balijas.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the Ustashas?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By "Ustashas," they meant the Croatian side. Sometimes they'd call them balijas, Turks, and Ustashas.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mean Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Look at page 5, the end of paragraph 53, where it is stated: "In the area of Birac, disarm or crush the remaining Ustasha forces." In the area of Birac, were there any Croats?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who inhabited the area of Birac?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What do you think, to who does this part of the order refer, where it says "disarm or crush remaining Ustasha forces"?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it refers to the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In connection with this directive by General Ratko Mladic, this directive issued by the Main Staff of Republika Srpska, did its implementation begin in early August 1993, in the area where you were?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've already stated, in connection with the earlier document, that it reflected the situation as it existed in my area, with the destruction of the Brosevici village. This particular document indicates that the intensity of the planning and implementation of these operations continues.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please make one correction to the transcript. My question to you was whether the directive of the Main Staff of Republika Srpska, the one issued by General Ratko Mladic, did its implementation begin in August 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is that how you understood my question?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Because it was erroneously entered into the transcript as 1993.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said early August 1992, but in my area, I experienced the same thing a couple of days earlier, which showed what our expectations could be.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please describe the atmosphere prevailing in the areas of Susnjari, Jaglici, and Brezova Njiva in early August 1992. What were things like there?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One cannot describe it in words. I don't know if I can make myself understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please answer my question, because of the time constraints. The events happening in the general area of Eastern Bosnia, could they have something to do with this directive, to your knowledge, whether there were such events, and did they affect your area?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very intense attacks commenced, both with artillery and infantry forces. Refugees coming from different directions started arriving in Susnjari, creating an atmosphere of chaos and fear.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Trial Chamber where the refugees were coming from in early August 1993, when they were coming to your area.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In June and July, the intensity from Vlasenica and Rogatica was somewhat weaker. However, from Zepa, Rogatica, and Gorazde, people started coming into our area. There were many of them. There was hunger, panic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you clearly when you said that there were refugees from Zepa, Gorazde, started arriving in your area in early August?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were some smaller groups arriving earlier, whereas others arrived in columns and in larger numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to accommodate all these refugees in your area?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They wanted to go either to Konjevic Polje, and therefore go across the area of Budim. They slept in forests, in sheds. And whoever found a shed was lucky. However, they were hungry, exhausted, and ill.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, did some of them move on to Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One could not keep these multitudes of desperate people under control.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you try to prevent them from going to Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please describe for the Trial Chamber one such instance of people on the move, going somewhere.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this time period, as far as I can remember, on the second or third, fourth, fifth, sixth -- or rather, all of these months, and especially -- therefore, from February, and especially in August, more than 5.000 desperate refugees from all areas of Bosnia; Gorazde, Visegrad, Zepa, Han Pijesak, Bratunac, Vlasenica, all of them flocked to our area and decided to move on to Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please pause.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although the witness was quite clear, it was entered into the transcript in a manner that does not make it clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about the period of the 1st of August up to some period in August of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. From the 1st to the 6th of August, 1992. I believe I made myself clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please focus on the following and describe for the Trial Chamber one such event involving a column of people.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If -- I will be able to describe it fully if I will be able to make myself do it. I will try. On the 6th of August, in the early morning hours, this multitude of desperate people decided to move on to Konjevic Polje across the mountain of Buljim and Ravna Gora, and they had to get past Hajducko Groblje, along the forward defence line of the Serb army, Hajducko Groblje, Siljkovici, they had to go along the eastern side, in the direction of north, and then on the other side, Bratunovici. That's an area of some 200 to 300 metres as the crow flies, but the refugees had to pass this stretch of land in the vicinity of the positions of the Serbian army. If we know that they were ambushed by groups of 10 to 15 people in different areas, then you know how difficult it must have been for them. And several thousand people headed on that day across Buljim, in the direction of Konjevic Polje. Despite the warnings and in spite of the fact that they knew what could happen to them, especially because a column of 1.000 to 1.500 people is quite visible, not just from up close but from afar, despite all of that, they headed out in the direction of Konjevic Polje. The column was a large one. There were women, children, and elderly there. As they arrived at Hajducko Groblje, they came under intense artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, Mr. Ademovic, where you were, and did you see that personally?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at such a vantage point that it was impossible for me not to see 1.500 people, and I was at Rupovici [phoen], which is an area overlooking the general region. And I was some 1.000 metres, at most, away, maybe some 700 to 800 metres, as the crow flies. And I had my binoculars. I could observe what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was going on?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the column came under intense artillery fire from the direction of Jezestica and Siljkovici, the artillery placed on Brzak also joined in. I could hear moans and some parts of the columns were massacred. Having seen what was going on, I set out with 15 of my men to help these poor people. As I reached the notorious Hajducko Groblje, which is the largest grave ever, I saw a terrible scene, but pulled myself together and opened fire upon the Serb forces, together with some of my 15 to 20 men. The area that divided me from the Serbian forces was about 100 metres. It was a clearing, and I could not advance any further. It was in this particular area that I witnessed such atrocious scenes that one would not wish upon one's greatest enemy. Dozens of dead, dozens of wounded. There was one thing that I found fascinating, and that was that in this nightmare of the wounded and dead, there was this old lady who survived the first onslaught, who got up on her feet and near to her I saw two boys who were some 8 to 10 years old. And I saw a Serbian soldier fire from a Zolja directly into the old lady, who was simply blown apart. She disappeared. After that, they opened infantry fire on the two boys, on the two children that I saw there. They were simply ripped apart with the bullets that were fired at them. It was then that I decided to come closer, along the left side, to come closer to the Serbian army. At that point, I wasn't thinking about getting killed. Together with my men, I intensified our fire. However, probably because we were short -- because they were short of ammunition and they didn't know how many of us there were, they retreated. Then I grabbed hold of an M-53 and some other infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ademovic. What were the consequences of this attack?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's finish this, because we need a break now. Yes, answer the question, please. What were the consequences of this attack? Very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just tell us the numbers.

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 40 and 50 killed, and as for the number of wounded, I don't remember it. There were both serious and light injuries. We pulled out the men who were with me and the refugees who joined us.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: How many civilians were there?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the column, they were all civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: But how many civilians were killed or wounded?

utterances.speaker: SIDIK ADEMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 40 and 50 were killed. Killed. But as for the number of injured or wounded, it was over a hundred, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll stop here. We'll take a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. Incidentally, because otherwise I would tend to forget: The document that you handed to us earlier on in the sitting, Mr. Di Fazio, regarding page 1 and now page 2, I think we ought to give it an exhibit number, and that will become Prosecution Exhibit P --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P589, Your Honour. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 589. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll reconvene in 30 minutes' time from now. That's 5 minutes after half past 4.00, 4.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ademovic, we were talking about the 6th of August, 1992, and you explained and described the consequences of the attack on the civilians on the 6th of August, 1992.
